desc:
Each item is given as [value, weight]. You have a bag that can carry total weight at most capacity. Unlike the 0/1 knapsack, items are divisible: you may take any fraction f (0 ≤ f ≤ 1) of an item, which adds f * value to your loot and f * weight to the load.

The best possible total value may not be an integer. Return it rounded down to the nearest integer.

items = [[60, 10], [100, 20], [120, 30]], capacity = 50   -> 240
items = [[10, 3]], capacity = 2                           -> 6   (2/3 of 10 is 6.67)
hints: If you could only take whole items this would be a hard problem. What changes when you can take parts?
Think of the value per unit of weight of each item. Where would you put your next unit of capacity?

Sort the items by value/weight in descending order (compare with cross-multiplication to avoid decimals). Take whole items while they fit; for the first item that does not fit take the fraction that fills the bag exactly. The answer is the whole values plus floor(value * remaining / weight).
editorial: Every unit of weight of item i is worth v_i / w_i. If a unit with a lower ratio is in the bag while a unit with a higher ratio is left out, swapping them increases the value, so an optimal bag takes items in descending ratio order. All items before the 'critical' item are taken whole, the critical item is taken partially, and the rest are ignored.

Sort by ratio using the comparison v_i * w_j > v_j * w_i (integers only). Let rem be the remaining capacity; if an item fits entirely add its value and subtract its weight, otherwise add floor(v * rem / w) and stop. Because the whole values are integers, flooring only the final fraction gives the floor of the total. O(n log n) time.
